Compared with the lower package (which protects Objective 3 but falls short on Objectives 1 and 2) and the ambitious package (which best achieves Objectives 1 and 2 but—under the 25% ceiling—leaves a material minority of low‑income households worse off on Objective 3), the targeted mid variant offers the most practicable balance across all four objectives given current constraints.  
Remaining risks/interdependencies: the realized congestion and emissions benefits depend critically on the Transit Agency delivering contracted frequency increases within its caps; revenue volatility, higher-than-expected admin/anti‑fraud costs, or greater behavioral responsiveness could reduce funds for transit and credits and threaten year‑3 neutrality; and businesses/delivery firms may face higher operating costs that require mitigation (time‑windowed deliveries, targeted exemptions, calibrated parking changes).  
For committee action I recommend endorsing the targeted‑credit mid variant, ring‑fencing net revenues to underwrite guaranteed transit frequency upgrades before full rollout, and requiring a 24‑month formal review (with pre‑specified metrics) to reassess the 25% ceiling and adjust design if equity or fiscal outcomes diverge from projections.
